new_statements.quote: Stress, length and nasalisation are not contrastive, whereas tone and intonation are. [...] A phonological word in Ama is defined as having one stressed syllable. Stress is in most cases predictable as it occurs on the heaviest syllable of the word. Heaviness is usually tied to vowel quality but sometimes to certain suffixes. There are certain words, however, where these two criteria fail to predict the stress. [...] The stress is usually placed on the heaviest syllable in the word. In Ama a heavy syllable is a syllable with a heavy nucleus consisting of a vowel that as part of its quality is louder and longer than other vowels in the same word. (p. 6)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Ama with an empty rule and no statements. Årsjö 1999 supplies the placement rule (heaviest syllable by a vowel-quality hierarchy, with a last-occurrence default when all vowels are of one kind), states stress is non-contrastive, and reports phonemic word tone (rising vs rising-falling on the last stressed syllable of 1–2 syllable words). Nothing in the catalog to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per phonological word; stress is non-contrastive and mostly predictable: it falls on the 'heaviest' syllable, where heaviness is a vowel-quality (sonority) hierarchy, from heaviest to lightest: /ai, au/ > /a/ > /əi, əu/ > /ɔ/ > /i/ > /u/ > /e, o/ > /ə/ (the schwa-like vowel written <o>; in the extracted text the legacy font renders it 'Å' and /ɔ/ as 'ç'). A syllable with /ə/ is stressed only if no other vowel is present. 'If a two or more syllable word contains only one kind of vowel the last occurrence tends to attract the stress' (p. 7), e.g. /unu/ [U'nu] 'shoot him', /isi/ [I'sI] 'garden'. Stress = loudness + length (stressed vowels are longer). Ama also has phonemic word tone: 'There is phonemic word tone contrasting on one and two syllable words. The contrastive patterns are a rising / and a rising-falling /\ tone on the last stressed syllable' (p. 8), e.g. /í:/ 'string bag' vs /î:/ 'tooth', /ə'mú:/ 'nose' vs /ə'mû:/ 'moon'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. A phonological word has exactly one (main) stress; complete reduplication 'gives two main stresses' and so 'results in two words' (p. 23).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) 'Heavy suffixes' that attract stress and 'bypass at least part of the above hierarchy': /-kə/ '3NS.U', /-kənə/ 'go down', /-jɔ/ 'moving towards', e.g. [fasI'kə] 'help them', [kåwI'jɔtUmɔ] 'bring him' (p. 7). (b) The inalienable-possession suffix /-tənə/ '3INAL' 'perturbs the stress so that it falls on the syllable immediately preceding it': /auwa/ ['auwa] 'my brother' vs /auwa-tənə/ [au'wat´nə] 'his/her brother' (p. 7). (c) Lexical exceptions: 'There are certain words that seem to be exceptions to the above stress rules, for example: /ewə/ [e'wə] 'water'' (p. 8). (d) Affixes and clitics 'carry no stress of their own' (fn. 10, p. 10).
new_statements.identity_note: Årsjö 1999 describes 'Ama, a Papuan language spoken in Papua New Guinea' (Left May family), based on SIL work at Ama village since about 1980 (the orthography 'used for the Ama language since 1980', p. 8); no dialect is singled out.

sources.quote: 'A phonological word in Ama is defined as having one stressed syllable. Stress is in most cases predictable as it occurs on the heaviest syllable of the word. Heaviness is usually tied to vowel quality but sometimes to certain suffixes. There are certain words, however, where these two criteria fail to predict the stress. There are two parts to stress in Ama: loudness and length' (p. 6). Hierarchy 'Starting with the heaviest vowel': /ai/, /au/ > /a/ > /ɒi/, /ɒu/ > /ɔ/ > /i/ > /u/ > /e/, /o/ > /ɒ/ (pp. 6-7) -- note this ORDER DIFFERS from the 1994 OPD (/i/,/e/ > /u/,/o/ > /ɒ/,/ɔ/): /ɔ/ is now a
